newsitem.title: SPAIN: Ex-fugitive renews Spain's "dirty war" accusations.
newsitem.headline: Ex-fugitive renews Spain's "dirty war" accusations.

text.p: Spain's disgraced former Civil Guard chief Luis Roldan broke a two-year media silence on Monday and re-asserted claims that the previous Socialist administration set up and covered up a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque separatists.

Once the country's most-wanted fugitive, Roldan told the daily newspaper El Mundo that former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez "knew everything" about the death squads, known as Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups (GAL), and attempts to cover them up.

"While I was in the Interior (ministry), the prime minister knew about all of the issues," Roldan told the paper in his first interview since fleeing the country in 1994. to escape a string of financial corruption charges
The ex-Civil Guard boss, captured by Spanish police and brought back to Madrid 10 months later to face embezzlement charges, spoke to El Mundo via a questionnaire sent to his prison cell.
He first made the claims about Gonzalez in a much-anticipated Supreme Court appearance in May, when he was answering a charge of involvement in the kidnapping of a Basque businessman.
Gonzalez has consistently denied any knowledge of the GAL and the Supreme Court recently decided there was not enough evidence to bring charges against the former premier.

Other high officials in the Socialist government, which ruled for 13 years before being defeated in elections last March under the shadow of the "dirty war" accusations, have been formally charged with involvement.
The Socialist Party quickly dismissed Roldan's accusations as pre-trial manoeuvres and statements by a non-credible source.

"Roldan is nearing his trial and he's trying to establish a line of defence, which is impossible to believe because he doesn't have one shred of credibility," Socialist spokeswoman Helga Soto told Reuters.

Roldan also accused three former state prosecutors of deliberately blocking investigations into the 1983-87 campaign of bombings, kidnappings, torture and murder that killed 28 presumed ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) activists.
He said the prosecutors had tried to keep two ex-police officers, Jose Amedo and Michel Dominguez, convicted in 1991 for involvement in GAL, from testifying against high-ranking officials.
"I have been at meals with the three state prosecutors whose only theme was a solution to Amedo and Dominguez," Roldan said.
"For what? In order for Amedo and Dominguez to keep covering up for those who were responsible for the GAL."

Roldan, himself a former Socialist, was the first civilian head of Spain's paramilitary Civil Guard. He has said he wants to speak out against politicians allegedly responsible for the GAL to avoid Civil Guard officers being used as scapegoats.
He has accused three former interior ministers in Gonzalez governments -- Jose Barrionuevo, Jose Luis Corcuera, Juan Alberto Belloch -- of being behind the death squads and the subsequent cover-up.

"The GAL was set up under the first interior minister (Barrionuevo). With Corcuera, everything was done to cover it up and in the third phase Belloch tried to clean up, sacrificing the pawns as usual," Roldan said.

Roldan's flight, amid accusations he made a fortune from kickbacks and secret funds diverted for his personal use, climaxed one of the biggest of a series of scandals which brought down the Socialist government.
ETA has killed some 800 people since starting a violent drive for Basque independence in 1968.
